OWNERSHIP OVER NATIVE C

An unconditional (ownership ...) form inside a native-c/1 unit makes its
preprocessed function bodies subject to ownership checking. The compiler and
readable export both run the check. Includes and active preprocessor branches
are read with the configured compiler flags, then bound and elaborated by the
existing C type layer. A #line directive cannot hide an unchecked definition.
The examples select C11: --std=c11 for export-c, or -std=c11 for cc. When the
compiler flags name no standard, the ownership check reads the unit as C11.

Example:

  (cesta native-c/1 compact-c/2
    (unit
      (ownership
        (check-all)
        (function find (returns-borrow 0 entries nullable))
        (function text (stores 1 static))
        (foreign report (variadic-read)
          (obligation "Reads its arguments during this call; retains none.")))
      ... C declarations and function bodies ...))

The representation and calling convention remain C's. Ownership bookkeeping
is erased. Bounds or arithmetic checks from checked-c/1 are a separate feature.
The native ownership profiles cover x86_64 SysV and AArch64 AAPCS64 LP64;
generated C carries target-specific static assertions for the selected profile. The mathematical
range and permission laws do not depend on a particular word size or ABI.

Certificate generation can stage individual function checks separately from
whole-module admission. A staged receipt reports module_admitted=false;
function certificates alone do not establish module admission. Resumption
reuses certificates only when their source, plan, checker and Lean dependencies
match, then checks the assembled module and reports module_admitted=true.

BORROWING

Pointer parameters borrow a complete pointee for the call. A pointer to const
borrows for reading; other pointers borrow exclusively. Passing two overlapping
exclusive arguments, or a shared and exclusive argument that overlap, fails.
Every call needs a checked body or an explicit foreign contract.

Checked switches accept grouped case/default labels sharing one body. Distinct
arms must not fall through into each other; the final arm may end normally.
Loop breaks inside an arm remain loop exits, and switch breaks exit that arm.

Every loop backedge must preserve its ownership and non-null entry facts.
The for-step is checked on continue paths as well as ordinary backedges.
Pointer guards are evaluated and refined on each iteration. A nullable entry
with a fresh guard can therefore remain valid while a non-null fact that the
body destroys is refused. Condition-false exits and break exits carry their
own resulting facts to the code following the loop; a break cannot weaken the
invariant used to check a continuing path.

A local pointer creates a lexical loan. A reborrow suspends its parent's
overlapping range. Distinct record fields can be used independently. A parent
becomes available again when its child scope ends. Shared loans can coexist.

Borrowed returns name an input index, optional member path and nullability:

  (function field (returns-borrow 0 member nested_member))
  (function find (returns-borrow 0 entries nullable))
  (function label (returns-static))
  (function maybe_label (returns-static nullable))

Input indices start at zero. The origin is the original input, so reassigning
a parameter cannot turn a local pointer into a valid return. A member path
narrows the caller's loan to that subobject. An unknown array index borrows
the whole inline array conservatively. Constant subscripts are range checked.
Dynamic subscripting through a raw pointer needs a checked bounded view.

A complete plain structure returned by value supports direct member reads,
including nested value members: make_result().ready and make_result().inner.tag.
The producer is checked once, including its argument loans and call effects.
Reference-bearing records, opaque capabilities and temporary array projections
do not use this rule; their lifetimes and release authority remain explicit.

A borrowed pointer result promises an origin, not an exact returned address.
The caller conservatively retains the declared footprint; it cannot infer a
remaining array length from an arbitrary interior pointer. Nonzero indexing
through such a result requires a bounded view instead.

BYTE VIEWS AND OWNING BUFFER RECORDS

  (view ReadBytes data len read)
  (view WriteBytes data len write)
  (view Buffer data len write (owns heap))

An optional element type extends the same declaration to scalar spans:

  (view ReadWords data len read u32)
  (view WordBuffer data len write u32 (owns heap))

Supported elements are bool, u8, u16, u32, u64 and usize. The pointer's C type
and width must match; bool is not interchangeable with u8. Lengths count elements.
The permission footprint records bytes, using checked count-times-stride
arithmetic. Copying another view's length retains its element count. The old
declarations without an element type retain their byte interpretation.

These name ordinary two-field structure typedefs: a byte pointer and an
unsigned size field. The record layout and ABI remain C's. Constructing a
view checks that its length fits a precise source extent. A known array
length, a constant allocation extent, or another checked view's length can
supply that extent. Pointer and length must be replaced together; independent
field updates and escaping their addresses are refused.
Volatile or atomic descriptor fields require a separate native resource
contract and cannot be declared as ordinary views.

Read views can share their data. Copying an exclusive view creates a reborrow
that suspends the source's overlapping access until the copy's scope ends.
An owning buffer holds the complete allocation and its release authority.
Moving that record moves the authority. Its data can be borrowed as a view;
release or another move is refused while the borrowed view lives. Release is
explicit, for example free(buffer.data). An owning buffer can also transfer
to an explicitly owned foreign parameter. No reference counter or destructor
is inserted.

  (function page_view (returns-borrow 0 bytes))

For a view result, this is an exact pointer/length contract for the declared
input subobject. The kernel checks exact extent on every recorded return.
It differs from an ordinary pointer result's lifetime-only promise.

Views pass by value to contracted checked-byte functions. Their recorded call
arguments lend the actual footprint, with read or write permission, while
the byte implementation retains its explicit runtime bounds checks. The
ByteViews example joins native record checking with checked-c/1 byte code.

Native functions can accept non-owning dynamic views and return the complete
view with (returns-borrow INPUT). The extent stays attached to the pointer.
Native code can inspect the descriptor and pass it to a contracted view
operation; indexing or dereferencing its dynamic data pointer directly is
refused, even at index zero. Use checked-c/1 accessors for those operations.
Passing that pointer to a fixed-pointee or variadic interface is also refused:
the view may be empty. Reconstructing a dynamic view from data and len requires
the same origin and element width; a constant length cannot shorten it.

Declared views nested in a (record ...) are atomic reference fields. They
inherit their view's read/write mode and require explicit initialization.
Their record result contracts name the whole view field:

  (view ReadWords data len read u32)
  (record Payload)
  (record Event)
  (function capture (returns-record ((firing words) (borrow 0))))
  (function store (stores-record 1 ((firing words) (borrow 0))))

Here Payload contains a ReadWords field named words, Event contains a Payload
field named firing, and input 0 is a ReadWords value. Nested record/array paths
retain the referent, not the temporary descriptor's storage. Both returned and
stored views must retain the complete declared input extent. Updating a view's
data or length independently, returning stack storage, and retaining a local
buffer after its scope ends are refused. A record pointer origin can name its
view field, for example (borrow 0 firing words).

cesta-ownership/4 makes the units explicit: whole-root and whole-view events
represent one complete dynamic input, and whole-viewed result shapes preserve
it. This unit is not a one-byte allocation. Lean interprets it at any caller
byte extent, including zero, while ordinary object roots retain byte units.
Admission rejects using a whole input in a fixed-size call or narrowing its
symbolic footprint. Earlier concrete-byte plans retain their interpretation.

Owned dynamic inputs, owning buffer results and owning nested views still
require allocation-extent contracts and remain refused by this profile.
Ordinary reference fields use the contracts below.

REFERENCE FIELDS

  (record Reader (field item (borrow read)))
  (record Writer (field item (borrow write)))
  (record Owner (field item (owns heap)))
  (record Label (field text (static nullable)))

These name complete ordinary structure typedefs. Every direct pointer field
has a declared lifetime and permission. Fields can be nullable. Borrowed
fields keep the referent alive; owning fields move its release authority.
Moving an owning record consumes its owning fields, and an unreleased field
prevents destruction of the containing allocation. Shared reference copies
keep the referent's lifetime rather than the lifetime of an intermediate copy.
Inline nested records use their own declarations. Inline arrays of declared
reference records apply those declarations pointwise, using the C array extent.
Positional element initializers and zero initialization are checked for every
element. Copying a containing owning record moves each element's release
authority; a second move is refused. Constant element projections preserve
their precise field ranges. Borrowing an unknown element conservatively
suspends overlapping access to the whole array. A direct unknown-index read of
a shared reference field checks every element for a common referent footprint,
or a static origin. It retains the referent's lifetime when the containing array
goes out of scope. The check does not invent per-index non-null facts; nullable
unknown-index reads retain nullability. Owning or exclusive field extraction,
ambiguous origins and unknown-index reference-field mutation remain refused.
Arrays of bare pointers need their own element interface and remain outside
this rule. Native ownership does not discharge dynamic numeric bounds: retain
the appropriate explicit guards or use checked bounded byte operations.

Calls carry the field permissions as well as the containing record's loan.
A const record parameter lends its fields for reading. Relational field
postconditions describe replacement or consumption through a record pointer:

  (function item (returns-borrow 0 item))
  (function replace (stores-field 0 item 1))
  (function set_label (stores-field 0 text static))
  (function consume_item (takes-field 0 item))

stores-field must establish the declared input lifetime on every return path.
takes-field consumes an owning field. A returned borrow never carries release
authority, including a mutable interior pointer from an owned record. Nested
output records and records returned by value use complete field interfaces.

Whole output records can name nested borrowed-field lifetimes:

  (function produce
    (stores-record 2
      ((firing item) (borrow 0 item))
      ((profile) (borrow 1))))

The output parameter is an exclusive pointer to an initialized reference record.
Every reference field of that record must appear exactly once. Paths traverse
inline records and constant array elements, for example (rows 1 item); they end
at a declared pointer field. A borrow origin with a path names the referent of
that input field, rather than the storage of its containing record. With no
path it names the ordinary input pointer. static remains an explicit origin.

Each return path must establish every postcondition. Local stack references,
wrong origins, incomplete field lists and ambiguous paths are refused. A caller
retains the referent's loan after the source record disappears, provided the
referent itself remains live. Repeated fields in arrays have distinct keys from
their ABI offsets. The emitted field signatures use the existing
independent field-postcondition checker. This form covers borrowed outputs;
owning fields through output pointers remain a separate extension.

Records returned by value declare their field origins directly:

  (function produce
    (returns-record
      ((firing item) (borrow 0 item))
      ((profile) (borrow 1))))

Initialization, assignment, direct forwarding of another call, and compound
literal returns carry the same contracts. All reference fields must be listed,
including inline array elements. A returned field retains the original input
referent; a local stack value cannot become a persistent result. Access rights
and nullability come from the record declaration. A returned record with live
owning fields cannot be overwritten or discarded.

Owning results transfer release authority once per field:

  (record Box (field item (owns heap nullable)))
  (function make (returns-record ((item) (owns heap))))

Each successful return consumes the callee's matching authority. Active borrows
prevent that transfer. A null field is allowed only when declared nullable.
The caller receives an owner of the complete pointee type and must release or
transfer it. Nested owning record arrays apply this rule to each element;
copying an already moved element is refused. Result contracts do not infer a
dynamic allocation extent from an arbitrary pointer field.

A conditional borrowed pointer or null retains the borrow's original lifetime
and becomes nullable. Dereferencing it requires a non-null guard. This rule
does not permit an optional owning-pointer copy; ownership needs an explicit
branch with a checked move. Returning a nullable pointer into a local object
is still refused.

OPAQUE CAPABILITIES

  (capability Ticket effects)
  (foreign issue (returns-own effects)
    (obligation "Issues a fresh valid permit for one logical call."))
  (foreign perform (owns 0 effects)
    (obligation "Consumes the permit and performs its call effect at most once."))

Ticket is a complete structure typedef whose representation is private to
checked clients. They use Ticket pointers; constructing a Ticket value,
accessing its fields, erasing a borrowed handle through an untyped interface,
or casting an unrelated allocation into a Ticket pointer is refused. An
owning Ticket field uses the same authority family. Moves and consumption
use the ordinary ownership rules, so readers cannot duplicate the permit.

Issuers and native consumers must implement the declared authority contract.
The declaration does not authenticate arbitrary bytes supplied by unchecked C
or add a runtime capability table. A native adapter can enforce identity and
revocation itself; checked clients retain the C representation and ABI.

GLOBAL CALL PERMISSIONS

A mutable file-local global names its owning function with (global name owner).
Direct calls determine a transitive effect graph, including recursive call
cycles. Each affected global is an implicit permission parameter of every
function that can reach its owner. Those parameters appear in signatures,
inputs and calls in the emitted plan; they do not change the C ABI.

A helper can therefore call a global owner, but cannot bypass a live loan by
re-entering that owner indirectly or carrying the alias in a record. Direct
source access remains confined to the declared owner. Native interface
obligations must account for callbacks and accesses outside their argument
footprints; unknown native implementations are not inspected by this graph.

Lean admission requires an empty ambient-permission list. A global permission
must be supplied through the call contract, like any other input permission.
Logical reference-field and global arguments precede scalar variadic arguments
in a plan. Scalar extras carry no permission; pointer extras require the
non-retaining read contract. C arity and value types are checked separately.

Nullable references require a non-null branch before access. Supported guards
include p, !p, p != 0, p == 0 and short-circuit combinations. Both branches
remain subject to ownership checking even when one test is a scalar constant.

OUTPUT POINTERS

  (function text (stores 1 static))
  (function select (stores 2 0))
  (foreign preserve_slot (preserves 0)
    (obligation "Preserves the stored pointer and its lifetime."))

The destination is a pointer-to-pointer parameter. Its result borrows static
data or the named input. Every returning or falling-through path must establish
the declared lifetime. A stored loan also constrains the callee while it is
live. At a call, the destination is an initialized local pointer slot.
Native mutable pointer-to-pointer arguments need either stores or preserves;
the checker never assumes that an arbitrary native write preserves a borrow.

CALLBACKS

  (callback Read (targets first second))
  (function apply (calls 0 Read))
  (record Cursor (field ctx (borrow read)) (field next (callback Read)))

A closed callback contract names a typedef of a nonvariadic function-pointer
prototype and the complete, nonempty set of functions that may flow into it.
Each target has a checked body, or an explicit foreign contract, with exactly
that prototype. All targets share one ownership contract, so a call through
the pointer is checked once against it. Targets receive their state through
explicit arguments: a function whose effects reach an owned global is refused
as a target.

A function name, with or without &, denotes that one function. A local
function pointer keeps the exact function it was assigned, and a call through
it is checked as a call to that function. A local pointer that hides a
function of the same name follows the pointer, not the name.

A function-pointer parameter needs (calls INDEX Name). A record field needs
the (callback Name) mode, or (callback Name nullable). A value may enter
either one when it is a listed target, or when it already carries a contract
whose targets are all listed. A nullable field may hold null; every other
position refuses it.

An invocation requires a callable known to be non-null, by its contract or by
a guard, and of the declared function type. A cast to another function type
is refused. The callable's storage is borrowed while the arguments are
evaluated, so an argument cannot replace the function being called.

Context lifetimes use the ordinary contracts. A borrowed context field keeps
its referent alive, a returned record names the input lifetime of each field,
and a result borrowed from the context blocks writes to it while live.
A callback that takes ownership of its argument consumes it at the call.

An open callback contract instead names an authoritative C record member:

  (callback ReadNext (field Cursor next) (returns-borrow 0 nullable))
  (record Cursor
    (field ctx (borrow read))
    (field next (callback ReadNext)))

The member must be a nonvariadic function pointer in a complete record. Its
actual C declaration supplies the prototype; the remaining clauses use the
ordinary foreign-function contract vocabulary. No function-pointer typedef or
duplicate C layout is required. Installing an implementation requires a checked
body or an explicit foreign contract, that exact prototype and a compatible
resource signature. A nonnull result may satisfy a nullable result; arguments,
origins, extents, access rights, allocation families and record postconditions
remain exact. An unchecked body is not a checked callback implementation.

An open interface cannot flow into a closed whitelist merely because its
prototype agrees. Entry-supplied callbacks remain named native obligations;
their C types do not establish arbitrary context invariants or imply that all
possible providers were checked. Context borrowing and result lifetimes still
use the ordinary rules above. Calls through a closed interface record every
possible target at the link boundary.
Link records also distinguish open interfaces from closed whitelists. Closed
targets are sorted by name, with translation-unit identity for internal-linkage
implementations. Reordering a whitelist preserves its contract; replacing it,
or substituting another unit's equally named static function, does not. A
closed interface containing internal targets cannot cross a unit boundary;
use an open contract for a shared implementation-independent interface. Rebuild
the link records when upgrading the checker so this evidence is present; older
callback records without provenance are refused. Associated callback contracts
travel with returned records and record pointers as well as parameters.

Closed callback plans use cesta-ownership/5 (or /6 for post-test control).
Plans with open interfaces use cesta-ownership/7, recording the interface's
foreign callable and actual implementation bindings. Older plans remain
admissible. The optional Lean checks admit those signatures and bindings in
the existing permission model; they do not interpret general C execution.

ALLOCATION, MOVE AND RELEASE

  (allocator heap malloc free
    (obligation "Allocates fresh storage of the requested extent; free consumes
                 its allocation once and accepts null."))
  (function consume (owns 0 heap))
  (function make (returns-own heap nullable))

The family is a nominal allocation/release identity. A local mutable pointer
initialized from an owned result becomes its owner. Initializing another
mutable pointer from that owner moves it; later use of the old binding fails.
A pointer to const borrows instead. &*owner explicitly reborrows for writing.

An owner must be released by its family's release interface or transferred to
an owned parameter/result. A live loan prevents moving or releasing its root.
An ordinary borrow has no release authority, even if it permits writes.
Overwriting or leaving an owner behind fails at compile time. Destruction is
explicit C code; the checker does not silently insert a deallocator.

This native profile admits constant allocation extents, including sizeof of
a complete record. Dynamic byte storage remains in checked-c/1 modules; their
interaction with native ownership currently needs a contracted native boundary.
A failed nullable allocation must also follow a
valid cleanup path; release(null) is part of the allocator contract above.

GLOBAL STATE

  (global state serve)

The global must have internal linkage. Only its declared owner function can
access it directly; helpers receive loans. A recursive call to the owner
cannot overlap a live loan of its global. Immutable scalar, array and record
constants can be read without a mutable owner. Mutable global references
cannot be returned as static references.

This is a sequential module discipline. Concurrency, interrupts and foreign
reentry require their own resource contracts; the declaration is not a mutex
or a proof of whole-program race freedom.

UNCHECKED DEFINITIONS

  (unchecked total (obligation "Reads count ints at values; callers pass an
                                array of that length."))

  (unchecked (pick_row last_row) (obligation "..."))

A function defined in the unit can be left out of the check by name, with the
fact its body relies on. Its callers are checked against its declared contract
exactly as for a foreign function, and the plan records it as a foreign
obligation. Contract parts (nullable, returns-borrow, stores and the others)
apply as usual. A pointer result may stay without an origin; a checked call
that receives it is then refused, and the plan omits that definition. A unit
may name every body unchecked; it then admits nothing as checked. A name
with no definition in the active preprocessing configuration has no effect:
a misspelt name leaves its body checked, and calls to a function that is only
declared still need a foreign contract. A parenthesized list of names shares
one contract and obligation. Declaring a
defined function foreign is refused: an unchecked body is always named.

CONTRACTS BESIDE A HEADER

  reader.h             the C declarations
  reader.h.ownership   (cesta ownership-interface/1
                         (record Reader (field bytes (borrow read)))
                         (function reader_peek (returns-borrow 0 bytes nullable))
                         (function reader_step)
                         (unchecked fence (obligation "...")))

A file named after a header, with .ownership appended, holds the contracts of
what that header declares. Every checked unit that reads the header, directly
or through another header, is checked with those contracts as if it had
written them. Such a unit needs no contract of its own for them:
(ownership (check-all)) is enough.

One text serves both sides of a call. In the unit that defines a function, a
(function NAME ...) contract governs the checked body. In a unit that only
declares it, the same contract governs each call; the plan records the call as
foreign, under the obligation that the definition meets the contract stated in
that file. (unchecked NAME ... (obligation "...")) names a native body once,
wherever the body appears: a static inline helper defined in the header stays
out of the check in every unit that includes it, and a unit that only declares
the name calls it under the same contract and obligation. (foreign NAME ...)
is a function with no checked body anywhere; a unit that defines it is refused.

record, view, callback, capability and allocator contracts apply in each unit
that declares their types and functions. An item whose type or function is
absent from a unit's preprocessing configuration has no effect there, and the
field contracts of a record that a unit sees only as an incomplete type have
nothing to govern in that unit. check-all, abi-fingerprint and global belong
to a unit and are refused in an interface.

A function has one contract. A unit item that states the same contract as an
interface item, with its name alone or in a group of names, is that same
contract. A different contract for the same function is refused, and so are
two interfaces that disagree. An error in an interface is reported with the
interface file's name and line; an error in a unit's own contract is reported
at that item.

  cesta export-interface [--cc COMPILER] [-o HEADER.ownership] HEADER UNIT.cesta [-- NATIVE-FLAGS]

writes the contracts a unit gives what HEADER declares, after checking the
unit: the record, view, capability and callback contracts of the header's
typedefs, an allocator whose functions it declares, and the contract of each
function it declares that the unit defines, checked or unchecked, or states
as foreign. A checked body with no contract of its own is written
(function NAME); a group of unchecked names is written name by name, each
with the group's obligation. The unit may keep its own items, which state the
same contracts, and writing the interface again gives the same text. An
obligation shared by a group often describes the unit rather than one
function; it is worth rewriting for each function in the interface.

A unit depends on each interface file it read: dependency output lists them,
the ABI fingerprint covers their contents, and cesta build checks the unit
again when one changes, or first appears beside a header the unit reads,
whatever its timestamp: the dependency record names the interfaces the last
check read. A make rule driven only by dependency files sees a changed
interface, and sees a new one when the unit is next rebuilt.

Whether a program links a definition checked under the same contract its
callers assumed is decided when the program is linked; see COMPOSITION AT
LINK TIME.

COMPOSITION AT LINK TIME

  cesta cc --contracts unit.o.contracts FLAGS -c unit.cesta -o unit.o
  cesta link-check [--obligations FILE] [--program NAME] RECORD...

A unit checked for ownership writes a link record. It names the functions
the unit defines, with their linkage and whether each body was checked or
left unchecked, and the functions the unit only declares but its checked
bodies call or name. Each carries its contract in a form that does not
depend on the unit: the signature the plan records, with allocator and
capability families and callbacks by name; the C function type, written
structurally, with an enumeration as its compatible integer type; the shared
contract of the targets of each callback it passes; and the layout of every
complete record its types reach. Effects on the unit's own private globals
stay with that unit; no other unit can reach them.

The link check reads the records of the units that make up one program.
Every call a checked body makes into another unit is matched with the
definition the program links:

- the definition was checked under a compatible contract: the call composes,
  and its foreign obligation is met by a checked body;
- the definition was checked under another contract, C type, callback
  contract or record layout: an error at the call, naming the definition and
  the first part that differs. A record that one unit saw only as an
  incomplete type has no layout to compare there;
- the definition is unchecked: the call rests on obligations, listed with
  the definition's own. If the call assumes another contract than the
  definition states, it rests on its own obligation; that is a warning, and
  the listing marks it;
- no Cesta unit of the program defines the function (C or assembly, a
  library, the linker): the call is listed as native, with its obligation.

Every unit of a program must be compiled for the same ABI model and plain
char. --obligations writes the list:

  (cesta link-obligations/1 (program "app") (units 2) (checked-calls 3)
    (native log_value (assumed "src/client.cesta" 30 "Writes ..."))
    (unchecked fence (defined "include/reader.h" 6 "An empty ...")))

Result refinement is deliberately bounded: a nonnull borrowed, static or owned
result satisfies the corresponding nullable result. All parameter requirements,
result origins and extents, rights, families and record effects stay equal.
The reverse direction is refused. C prototypes, callback interfaces and shared
complete record layouts must still agree.

The optional ownership-composition model connects compatible contracts to
admitted permission bodies and proves that call effects and permitted returns
respect the caller's contract. A checked flag without body evidence does not
close a call in that model. Qualification consumes actual emitted records and
body plans, with allocation-family names interned across units. Private-state
framing, source projection, native obligations, actual linker selection and
compiler fidelity remain separate boundaries. This is not a proof of general
C execution or of an arbitrary complete executable.

cesta build does this for every program it links. An authored source writes
its record beside its object (OUT/TARGET/obj/SOURCE.o.contracts), an archive
carries its members' records beside it (LIBRARY.a.contracts), and the records
of archives and objects among a program's link inputs take part. A program is
linked only when its records compose; its list is written to
OUT/TARGET/TARGET.obligations. A make-driven build runs cesta link-check
itself.

Contracts are compared as resolved, not as written: (function f) in one unit
and (foreign f (obligation "...")) in another are one contract. They are
compared for equality: a caller that assumes less than a checked definition
provides (a nullable result that is never null) is reported as a difference.
The linked definition is the program's own object first, then its inputs in
link order; a definition the linker would choose otherwise (weak symbols, a
library found by search) is outside the check. A unit with no ownership
declaration has no record, and its functions are native to the check.

SURVEYS

CESTA_OWNERSHIP_SURVEY=FILE makes the check continue past a refused function
body. Each refused body appends one line to FILE: the unit's source identity,
the function name and its first refusal, separated by tabs.
A surveyed unit is never admitted: the command fails, reporting how many of
its bodies were refused.

REFUSALS AND THE IMPLEMENTATION BOUNDARY

The current surface admits inline value records and arrays and references to
them, declared views, reference fields and opaque handles as described above.
Unions, bit-fields, pointer reinterpretation, integer-manufactured
pointers, indirect calls, unsupported control transfers and uncontracted native
calls are refused inside the checked region. Volatile and atomic memory are
accessed through named native resource contracts.

Ordinary C scalar computations, initialization of all individual subfields,
and all dynamic array bounds are not proved by this pass. It does not make
arbitrary C free of undefined behavior. Checked byte functions provide runtime
bounds and arithmetic checks where those are needed. Source projection, ABI
layout calculation, printing and compilation remain tested boundaries.

PROOF RECORDS

  cesta export-c source.cesta --std=c11 --plan source.plan -o source.c

The ownership record includes actual allocation ranges, loan creation and end,
accesses, branches, loops, move/release/transfer events, result contracts and
named foreign obligations. OwnershipPlans checks the independent spatial
invariant. PermissionFlow covers every finite execution, with a failed
permission operation represented as a fault. OwnershipAdmission proves fault
avoidance and result cleanup for admitted recorded programs. Foreign behavior
and the C-to-plan projection are separate obligations.

Equal permission states are merged during admission, without merging program
values or runtime answers. Membership preservation proves that neither branch
nor any loop execution is lost. Function proofs are checked separately and
joined by a proved module rule, avoiding one large admission computation.

The cesta-ownership/2 record includes typed callable signatures, parameter
root bindings, ambient private roots and actual call arguments. Kernel
admission checks extent and access rights at a call, validates input roots
against the signature, and relates returned lifetimes to the original inputs.
An owner consumed for an argument leaves a receipt that only the matching
call can consume; a pending receipt prevents successful function return.
Foreign parameter effects and implementation behavior remain named obligations.
Recorded field postconditions include their destination keys and original
input lifetimes. Kernel admission checks that every return supplies them;
changed keys, origins, extents and omitted field results are refused.
New plans emit cesta-ownership/3. It adds
field-offset result signatures, borrowed/static result observations and owning
field transfers. Admission checks complete unique result keys, original input
lifetimes, matching allocator families and consumption of every returned owner.
Existing cesta-ownership/2 plans remain accepted by the admission runner.
Pointer-to-pointer stores/preserves postconditions are still checked by the
native frontend; their full relational postcondition is not yet in this plan.

ABI AND HEADER BINDING

Use ordinary #include declarations to import a native library's public types.
The ownership checker reads those actual headers through the selected compiler
environment; a second copy of the library's typedefs is not an ABI witness.

The plan contains one cesta-abi/2 SHA-256 fingerprint, along with its readable
target, record sizes/alignments/field offsets, callable parameter/result layouts,
and native-view element widths. The fingerprint covers that layout, the tokens
of the preprocessed translation unit, the contents of the headers actually
read, and the contents of the interface files beside them. Whitespace between
the unit's tokens is not part of it, so a pin taken from an exported plan also
holds when the same unit is compiled. Input chunks are length delimited. Header paths are not hashed, so moving a
source tree without changing its contents preserves the fingerprint unless
the program itself observes a path through a C macro such as __FILE__.

An optional contract pins the previously inspected interface:

  (abi-fingerprint "64 lowercase hexadecimal digits from the emitted plan")

Compiling or exporting that checked unit recomputes the fingerprint and refuses
a changed header, target or source. The clause is excluded from its own input.
To adopt an intentional interface change, omit the pin, inspect the regenerated
layout and plan, then use the new fingerprint. Ordinary unannotated C requires
no pin and continues to delegate to the C compiler.

The fingerprint detects drift; it is neither a signature nor a proof of the
C layout algorithm. Lean admission checks the recorded permission program.
Native header binding is established by regenerating that plan in its actual
compiler environment. The compiler and C-to-plan projection remain separate
qualification boundaries.

The underlying CMemory heap is parametric in its cell permission algebra.
Exclusive cells and fractional read permissions are existing instances. The
borrow theory distinguishes allocation lifetime, access permission and release
authority. BorrowingLayouts connects subobject ranges to the existing padded
record and array layout laws. The native surface is deliberately a conservative
instance of this more general theory.

ADMISSION CHECKPOINTS

The actual-plan admission runner reuses a compiled proof only when its plan,
generated proof source, generator, model artifacts, toolchain and proof artifact
fingerprints match. Changes invalidate the checkpoint. --no-cache forces fresh
kernel checks. Checkpoints are build artifacts and add no runtime mechanism.

REFERENCES

RustBelt: https://plv.mpi-sws.org/rustbelt/popl18/paper.pdf
Oxide: https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.00982
Tree Borrows: https://research.ralfj.de/papers/2025-pldi-tree-borrows.pdf
Mezzo: https://cambium.inria.fr/~fpottier/publis/pottier-protzenko-mezzo.pdf
Cyclone regions: https://www.cs.cornell.edu/projects/cyclone/papers/cyclone-regions.pdf
Cogent: https://trustworthy.systems/publications/papers/OConnor_CRJAKMSK_21.pdf

These motivate resource interpretations, source-level loans and the separation
between a borrow checker and an unsafe aliasing semantics. This implementation
does not claim to implement or prove any of those complete systems. Mezzo's
field permissions, Cyclone's separation of regions from allocation policy and
Cogent's explicit refinement boundary inform this compositional design.

ANALYSIS PRECISION

Branch and loop joins currently require compatible ownership, reference
origins and live loans. A future precision extension is a bounded domain of
guarded alternatives, retaining which origin/permission holds under each
stable predicate. This is planned analysis work, not an admitted construct.

For example, choosing p=&a under g and p=&b under !g can justify writing the
other object under the same unchanged guard. Changing g, mutating a predicate's
dependencies through an alias, or revoking a supporting grant must destroy that
correlation before reuse. Guard identity therefore includes dependency versions,
not just source spelling. A domain limit must lose precision conservatively;
it cannot discard feasible executions or infer their impossibility.

Admission requires a concrete interpretation and sound transfer/join rules,
then actual-plan integration. Controls must accept stable correlated disjoint
access and refuse overlapping access after guard mutation, dangling branches,
duplicated ownership and stale authority. Bounds, protocol facts and compiler
hints must retain their own preservation laws and native assumptions.

SWITCH EXITS

A switch containing a default label emits switch-total: every admitted arm is
possible, without an invented no-match path. Returning arms remain terminal;
break arms resume after the switch. Without default, the no-match path remains.
Nested switch and loop exits retain their own target. These are ownership-plan
control-flow facts, not a functional-correctness proof of the C implementation.

POST-TEST LOOPS AND CLEANUP JUMPS

Native ownership accepts do ... while, including do { ... } while (0) helper
macros. The first body executes before its condition. Continue leaves the
body's inner scope and reaches that condition; break skips the condition.
An outer variable initialized on every first-iteration exit is available
afterward. A constant-false condition requires no repeat invariant, so a
single-iteration body may consume an owner. Otherwise the repeated body and
condition must preserve the permissions at the repeat edge.

Forward goto may target a label directly in the function's outer compound
body. Jumps from nested blocks, loops and switch arms are supported. The
checker ends loans in exited inner scopes, then checks the cleanup tail with
the resources actually held on that incoming path:

  int *p = reserve(sizeof(int));
  if (!p) { dispose(p); return 0; }
  int *q = reserve(sizeof(int));
  if (!q) { dispose(q); goto out_p; }
  ...
  dispose(q);
out_p:
  dispose(p);
  return 1;

The tail is checked separately for each incoming path. An allocation cannot
vanish at the jump, a released owner cannot be released again, and a loan
cannot outlive the scope it leaves. A bypassed fixed-size declaration creates
uninitialized storage at the label without executing its initializer. Reading
it before an assignment is refused.

Backward jumps, computed jumps and jumps into a nested block require further
control-flow contracts and are refused by this ownership profile. Ordinary C
compilation still accepts the native compiler's full control-flow language.

Post-test bodies emit cesta-ownership/6 plans. Mandatory-body and latch records
lower to the existing permission plan using PermissionIteration.resumeIteration;
its execution law preserves return, break and continue targets, including
nested branches and loops. Forward cleanup jumps record the tail's permission
actions at the jump site. Neither lowering rewrites the emitted C control flow.
